Industry News: Jon Gustin, The Tired Dad, On the Manosphere, Stoicism, and Showing Up

📅 05 May 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How do you make the The Tired Dad perk up?
  • To the contrary, Gustin, better known as The Tired Dad, holds up his fatigue as a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.” Tiredness is his brand, sure, but it’s also a conversation starter — a way to assess and unpack the strain that kids, relationships, work, and showing up for your family can put on you.
  • Gustin’s social feed is something of a sacred space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do you make the The Tired Dad perk up? Get vulnerable.

Jon Gustin is tired. But he's not complaining. To the contrary, Gustin, better known as The Tired Dad, holds up his fatigue as a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.” Tiredness is his brand, sure, but it’s also a conversation starter — a way to assess and unpack the strain that kids, relationships, work, and showing up for your family can put on you.

Gustin’s social feed is something of a sacred space. There’s a melancholy confessional aspect to it, in which he offers statements like, “I’m constantly thinking about what I’m leaving behind…” Yes, it’s a familiar sentiment, but one that we rarely dare to face straight-on. In this sense, The Tired Dad feels nearly dystopian, like Gustin is playing the role of the protagonist in Lois Lowry’s The Giver, the Receiver of Memory who takes on the pains that those in society do not face. But then, out of darkness, there is Gustin as motivational speaker, coach, and teacher. In facing the darkness, he finds the light. He ends most posts with a mantra such as, “Keep showing up.”.

Recent findings suggest that gustin has taken his social media philosophizing and translated it to a book, The Tired Dad: 100 Reflections on Showing Up for What Matters Most, out now. Inside, you’ll find fleshed-out contemplations and personal histories and, of course, plenty of advice on being a man, sobriety, marriage, fatherhood, and vulnerability.

According to recent reports, just a week out from his book release, I had the chance to talk with Gustin. He didn’t come ready to push his book — with the influencer energy you might expect — but with his signature sincerity that, I realized, is part of his practice. "Vulnerability is freedom," Gustin tells me shortly into our discussion. "And not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone." Here, to help us all feel a little less alone, is our full conversation.

This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

According to recent reports, jon Gustin: I like to bring up the fact that my dad entered the Marine Corps at the ripe age of 17. His parents had to sign for him and he was in Vietnam by the time he was 18 and he spent just over two years there. It's hard to wrap my mind around that.

Industry observers note that the number one thing he's taught me is character. And he learned that from his dad, who was in World War II in the Navy. I come from a very military background, very structured, and with men that don’t show much emotion. I think I've seen my dad cry about five times, and three in maybe the past couple years. But he always taught me about character, saying stuff like, "If you say you're going to do something, do it." True character is when no one's looking, you always do the right thing. And not only did my dad and grandpa say that stuff, they highlighted it every single day in their actions. If he remarked he was going to play catch with me or go to something, he would make it happen. So that's kind of my dad in a nutshell.

In the book, it’s clear you held your grandfather in great esteem. Tell me about him as a role model.

According to recent reports, when I was writing this book, my grandfather passed away, at the age of 99. And that passage I wrote in the book was right after he passed. Towards the end of his life, he was so unfiltered, but in a good way. He almost got more emotional and more expressive because I don't think he had that shield up anymore. And it was just kind of, he didn't care. And the way he talked about my grandmother and their marriage and just how much they loved each other is like a storybook.

My whole life, my grandfather was just a man of wisdom. He knew so much. He read the newspaper every day. He would read two books in a day. It was insane. So he was just full of wisdom and insight. And he didn't care about the stupid stuff in life, like the material things. It was always strictly like, who you are as a man, like truly, who are you?

There's so many moments with my grandfather and the way he was. It was a different generation. So not too much expressive emotion there, but very, very kind. He always treated people so well. He was always there for us. They bought a motor home after retirement and they traveled everywhere to see all the grandkids and the great-grandkids and the whole family. And that's how they spent their money and their time. And they spent their money helping people out with donations. They would get audited all the time because they donated so much of their money that the government didn't believe in them. So that's who they were.

I'm wondering what you think of those men out there who have not had such role models. Absenteeism is a stubborn problem in this country ...

Sources indicate that I think fathers are such a vital, vital role in the dynamic of family. But even with the absenteeism, I know some fellow friends and stuff that had horrible relationships with their father or didn't have them at all, but they are the greatest fathers themselves. And they really are using that as motivation to just put their foot down and break that curse and to show up for the first time in their family — to be that shift in generational trauma, I guess. And it's weird to view myself as a role model just because I'm not perfect and I have made so many mistakes in my life early on, but I think I do want to be.

Recent findings suggest that as I say in the book, vulnerability is freedom and not only is it freedom for yourself to be vulnerable, but it's freedom for other people because they feel less alone. If you can express yourself, then other dads, other people will say, "Oh, I thought I was alone in that. But this person's expressing that. I must not be crazy." And it kind of frees them up. So if anything, I want to be just a role model to be vulnerable in your story and that we don't always have it figured out and that the point is not to figure it all out. The point is to be on a journey forever and to always be progressing towards something and to lead with wisdom and intentionality to be role models to your kids and as a side effect, to be a role model to others.

Industry observers note that vulnerability is at the core of what you put out there. Given that, I wonder what you think of stoicism. It's historically seen as a masculine trait and while is has been vilified for the repression of emotion, it seems to be getting a second look, especially with so many kids struggling with independence, perseverance, and resilience. I'm curious as to what you think about it and when to go vulnerable and when to go Stoic.

According to recent reports, I sat down with Ryan Holiday not too long ago and I've always read his stuff. And before I kind of knew Ryan Holiday and his message of stoicism, the modern message of stoicism, I did just think it was this overly masculine thing — like, we are statues, we're Greek Gods who must keep chipping away. And it wasn't until I started to really dive into it and learn that, at least what Ryan preaches, that there is vulnerability in stoicism. Perseverance is great, but I still think there's an aspect of saying, "Hey, you know what? I'm defeated and I don't know." It’s okay if you don't have the answers. I think men want to fix everything and have the answers and they feel like they're dumb or they are weak if they don't have the answers. And I think that vulnerability of saying, "I don't have the answers.".

Sources indicate that and there's some extremes to stoicism. When the world is gladiator brutal, when Marcus Aurelius put his kids to bed every night as if he's never going to see them again. I don't think it's healthy to have that extreme a mentality. The whole memento mori, I wrote about it in the book — I want to think about it a little differently. I don't want to think about dying all the time. Sometimes I want to think about dying at 100 and living like I'm going to live to 100 because as I mentioned in the book, if you told me I was going to die tomorrow, yes, I would live my day today a lot differently, but chances are I'm probably not going to die tomorrow. I think men want this black and white way of thinking, and sometimes it's just not that way.

And that's, again, men want to have this identity, right? Warrior, Spartan, Stoic, man. We want to be part of this group. I listen to Joe Rogan. I do jiu-jitsu. I do cold plunges, which I do all of those, but it's not my entire identity. Sometimes it can be your identity masking your true identity, your insecurities, your ego and everything like that.

Speaking to those extremes and that black and white thinking, what do you make of the more extreme corners of the manosphere?

I mean, the manosphere is birthed from insecurity. It's birthed from lack of identity. I speak from experience because in my early 20s ... I guess I was part of the manosphere before it was called that. I thought, I'm going to be a man. I'm going to view myself very highly and I'm going to be egotistical, but think I'm being manly. And there were mentors in my life too that were like that.

Industry observers note that and that I saw these men that were just powerful, but they were something, there was a red flag that I was like, they seem so insecure. Seem like they're overcompensating for something. And then they don't seem like they're like the greatest of husbands. And I was young, I was in my 20s so, but I could see so easily how impressionable young men can be on this manosphere type mentality because they're just looking for identity and they're so insecure and they really don't know how to talk to girls.

Industry observers note that so if they just view girls as less than, then they can have power over them. And if they just become successful with money, then they can have power over people and there's no substance to it, but it's a search for identity of what masculinity is. And when you see this facade of masculinity, these guys with deep voices that talk real loud and are on steroids and it could like, okay, yeah, that's what I want.

I look back on it, the things I valued as early 20s and now 20 years later, I mean, it's not even close. I'm like, "That's not what I value at all." Now, I value time and that's the greatest currency. Money is important clearly to an extent, but the obsession with money is empty and there's no cars that are going to fulfill you. There's no amount of women that's going to fulfill you. Actually, it does the opposite. And until you see that for yourself and other people or maybe experience it yourself, you realize that, yeah, this isn't masculine at all. This is weakness because, you're actually very weak and you’re overcompensating for all your insecurities.

Recent findings suggest that growth is hard. Do you see yourself as an expert in parenting, masculinity, relationships?

It has been revealed that no, I'm not an expert in any of it. Expert is a funny word. To call yourself an expert makes you feel like you've reached the end. And I don't believe that there is an end until the end of there's always something to learn, there's always something to get better at. There's always something new to read. There's always more information. There's always something. So no, I don't consider myself an expert at all. I'm learning as I go.

Relationships get hard when you have kids. I think that's a fact of life and something you address a lot. For those newly introducing kids to their marriage, where can they start when the going gets hard?

Recent findings suggest that kids changed marriage completely. There are a lot of curve-balls there, but communication is huge. Kill your ego. Ego serves absolutely no purpose in a relationship. Meet the other person where they are, rather than trying to fix them. The other person's not going to fix themselves for you. You're going to fix yourself for the other person. Both of you fix yourselves to meet the other person, right, and to accept the other person and to work with the other person as teammates, not as competitors, because in competition you'll lose. It's just a lose-lose. Nobody wins in that.

Recent findings suggest that so I think it's effective communication, vulnerable communication. Because it's not just communicating — just complaining about the other person, that's not effective communication. Effective communication is where the other person doesn't get defensive. You're not attacking them. You're trying to solve a problem. And once you kill your ego and stop being so defensive to everything, you guys can start communicating in an effective way, and then that's where the growth happens.

I see these days more men on the playgrounds, more men parenting in public spaces. But I still don’t see, well, full participation in parenting. I'm part of the PTA, for example, and am often the only dad in the room. Sometimes I go to the pediatrician and am the only dad taking my kids there. What would you like to push men to do more of?

Industry observers note that well, just to get out of that idea that your only job is a financial provider. You work and when you're done with work, you're done with work. I want fathers to view their role as a dad just as crucial, probably more important than their work job, than their job title. When you come home, you need to put on your other cap, which is dad, and that's your most important role. So the work doesn't stop. It's why we're so tired because the work never stops.

Sources indicate that my wife and I are transplants. I'm from California. She's from Ohio, and we met in Tennessee and started our family here. Nobody around, no village per se. And I think sometimes it was so hard that I got resentful of other people who had helpful grandparents nearby.

But now I look back on it and realize it made me a better dad to force myself to wake up so early in the morning and then come home and watch my kids and then go back to work and play this tag team with my wife. It was draining and hard, but now I look at it as kind of a blessing. Because first of all, I have a ton of memories with my kids growing up. I think my kids will think I was with them 24/7 because I am with them so much. There are times when, okay, I'm canceling my clients. I'm losing money today because my kid is sick. I got to take him to the pediatrician. My wife can't take off work. It is what it is. And that's just made me so much of a better dad.

In a recent development, and that's the badge of honor of a tired dad, that we wear because we're showing up in all areas. We are showing up to work, but we're showing up until we put our heads down.

Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.
  • Industry observers note that two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth.
  • It has been revealed that the studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Industry observers note that two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

It has been revealed that the studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

Recent findings suggest that the second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Recent findings suggest that both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

In a recent development, “Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Sources indicate that parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

In a recent development, according to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

Sources indicate that A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”.

It has been revealed that it’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

This article was originally published on November 6, 2026.

Ty Burrell Has Some Advice For Parents of Teens

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.
  • In a recent development, let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen.
  • Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.

In a recent development, let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen. He’s just that kind of guy — disarmingly affable and sincere and funny. This is a good thing because right now he’s talking about meningitis. Yes, meningitis, that overlooked infection that, you probably didn’t know, kills 1 in 10 who develop it with 1 in 5 having long-term health consequences like brain damage and hearing loss. Also, kids age 16 to 23 have the highest rates of it. And that’s what brings us here with Burrell, a dad of two teens, and a message. In partnership with GSK (for the Ask2BSure campaign) Burrell has teamed up once again with Julie Bowen and a stand-in teen actor (mom and dad are back!) to give awareness and, yes, make jokes.

Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).

So … Why are you, Ty Burrell, America’s dad, talking about meningitis?

Well, it's pretty organic, actually. I have teenage girls, and unfortunately, the most vulnerable population is, actually, I guess, teens to college, 16 to 23. And that's doing large part to the teen lifestyle. My girls play sports, and there's a lot of water bottle swapping. And once you're in college, it's dorm rooms and it's kissing and all of it. And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

But meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. So that's why I'm partnering with GSK on the Ask2BSure campaign to raise awareness about meningococcal disease or meningitis.

To that end, we made a video that we hope is funny, kind of a lighthearted way to educate people and inform people.

In a recent development, it is funny! But I must say as a parent of a 14-year-old, I almost couldn't get the humor because I got afraid.

Yeah, I know. It's a tightrope walk, isn't It?

I happened to have a doctor check in with my 14-year-old this week and I asked them about meningitis. It turns out that I'm two years early. So I'm wondering outside of this PSA, which I think will get people asking doctors, what basic things should parents of teens know.

Well, I would direct them to a healthcare professional in terms of all of the basics. But what I know is that the vaccines available, in terms of strains, A, B, C, W, and Y, but a lot of teens don't have the meningitis B vaccination. And that was true of my 16-year-old. And I did the same thing. When I started to learn more about how serious this was, I had a conversation with our doctor and she hadn't had B yet, so that's now scheduled. And I mean, as far as my knowledge about it, it would be that and really just encouraging people to have a conversation with their doctor about the risks of meningitis and about vaccination, and if that's an option.

It is that simple. I was wondering, I mean, we dads, are always look for a way to make something into a lecture... Is there a way to segue from the meningitis talk or explanation to other necessary talks?

You do have to say it's because you're probably going to be making out with people.

Yeah, totally. I don't know what it's like for you, but I feel like the window in which I actually have any influence for them is three sentences. And I don't know if that's a lack of attention span because of phones or screens or what have you, or it's just time-honored parenting, that you just have the floor for a brief moment before you are tuned out.

It has been revealed that “This very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy.”.

And their brains short-circuit.

Totally. And get frustrated fast. It's a lecture. We're now in a lecture. So I don't know about the segueing into a separate topic, but I will say that my wife, luckily, with girls is taking the conversation off of my plate.

In a recent development, oh great. You can just tell them how dirty dorm rooms are.

Industry observers note that that's the dad's role. So you have two teens now. What's the toughest things you've found about raising them and maybe what's the best?

According to recent reports, for the baby or toddler on your holiday list, a Lovevery Play Kit is genuinely one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each kit is developmentally designed by experts for a specific age and stage, so every single toy inside has a real purpose and actually supports what that child’s brain is working on right now. The Free Spirit Kit is designed for older toddlers exploring independence, creativity, and imaginative play, and it comes with everything from open-ended building materials to pretend play pieces that grow with them well beyond the holiday season. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

The Sticki Rolls capsule series has absolutely taken over my daughter’s friend group, so she will lose her mind when she sees Series 3 under the tree. Each roll is a peel-and-stick experience that reveals collectible band stickers inside, and the trading, collecting, and comparing with friends has become a whole social event in itself. They are the kind of small, inexpensive gift that delivers an enormous reaction, which is the ideal holiday gift math. It’s the perfect stocking stuffer or add-on for any kid who is deep in the sticker and collectible era right now! — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, this is the holiday gift that every parent who is trying to delay handing their kid a smartphone needs to know about. The Tin Can is a Wi-Fi landline designed specifically for kids, with no screen, no apps, no social media, no browser, and no strangers getting through. You control the approved contact list from the app, kids can call friends and family with real voice calls, and there is even a free Can-to-Can plan so two Tin Can kids can call each other for free with no subscription required. It’s designed for kids 4 and up, requires zero power tools or adult intervention once they gets the hang of it, and the independent building projects it unlocks are genuinely impressive. — Katie Garrity.

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow).

But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also shows how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter indicates he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”.

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it.".

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”.

It has been revealed that then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

It has been revealed that llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a big role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas indicates, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”.

Sources indicate that tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”.

According to recent reports, tom Llamas and family. Credit: NBC.

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”.

Llamas indicates he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in Fresh York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”.

This Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

In a recent development, back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

Most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and significant enough to get them through practice.

In a recent development, the 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. No wardrobe overhaul needed, just a few clever pieces to make her feel more put together.

Listen. Moms are juggling about a million things every minute of every day. So, yeah, maybe we reach for the same outfit or some spin on it every time we leave the house. Our unofficial uniform most days is black yoga pants and an oversized sweatshirt. And, sure, there are many days when we look like Adam Sandler's stunt double rolling through the school pickup line. Hey, whatever; it works. It's comfy and reliable.

That doesn't mean that even the most prolific outfit repeater hasn't caught a stray glimpse of herself in the mirror and thought, Hmm, my wardrobe could use a little love. Enter: these gifts. Trust, we're not here to talk anyone out of their uniform. (Respectfully, we would never.) We’re just talking about giving her a few pieces that will make her feel fresh and more put-together on the days she wants to try something different. A statement boot, a chic pullover, a bandana for a pop of print, jewelry she’ll never take off: small swaps that turn “I just threw this on” into “This is exactly the look I was going for” without a ton of effort or extra thought.

The brown colorway is warm and versatile enough to work year-round, and the quality is genuinely impressive. One wrap, infinite outfits, zero effort... exactly the kind of upgrade a mom who has better things to think about actually needs. — Katie Garrity.

I’ve long believed that a good pair of boots can make any woman feel like a total put-together badass, but I’m over 40 now... boots can’t just be aesthetic; they also have to be comfortable. I love that these have the edge of a classic moto boot (adjustable buckle straps, a chunky lug sole), with the added benefit of a cushioned insole and lightweight sole so they’re actually wearable all day long. They look AND feel great. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I am obsessed with this bracelet. It's handmade using over 1,200 beads and is just so stunningly beautiful. I love how it goes with everything, and I can't leave the house without people complimenting it. In a world where I'm often wondering how my jewelry is sourced, I can feel so good about this piece every time I look at it. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that this necklace has become one of my most-worn pieces! The Waterdrop is a delicate, perfectly shaped teardrop pendant that hits that sweet spot of simple enough to wear every day but special enough to actually feel like jewelry. The quality is genuinely impressive, the weight of it feels substantial and real on the neck, and it layers beautifully if you are a stacker or looks just as good worn alone. For the woman on your holiday list who appreciates understated, elegant pieces she will actually reach for constantly, this is such a thoughtful and beautiful gift. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that I got a compliment on this Varley half-zip literally the first time I wore it (shoutout to my boss for noticing), so it’s already earned its keep. It’s cozy enough for the routine stuff like kid errands and carpool, but the two-tone ribbed fabric and stand collar make it look way more intentional than my old basic sweatshirt. It hits that sweet spot of comfy and put-together every mom is looking for. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite outfit hacks is wearing something really simple, like a white T-shirt and jeans with a really fun pair of sneakers. Enter these fun sneakers. I already love my Gola Elan sneakers, and now they come in fun animal prints that I can't get enough of. I chose the cheetah, but the cow and the dalmatian picks look just as awesome. If you often wear a "uniform," this is a great way to mix it up just a bit. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that these are on my wish list because dark green satin pants make a plain sweater look like a whole holiday look. They’re pull-on with an elastic waistband, so they’re basically fancy pajamas that are still special enough for the party invitation, and the 3% spandex gives them a little stretch for dinner-table lingering. At $98, they’re a pretty easy way to get a brand-latest outfit out of the one top she already loves! — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that I discovered the Varley brand on a casual browse of Evereve, hence my newfound obsession with their half-zips! The Maura is the slightly dressier sister to the Milano half-zip, making it the perfect pairing for high-rise jeans or wide-leg trousers. I have a long torso and the cropped, relaxed fit doesn’t feel too short, which is a huge bonus, and I’m obsessed with the foldover collar. — Julie Sprankles.

I love the distinct look of this bag, along with the really neat way that the straps convert from handles to an adjustable cross-body length. The size is also perfect for carrying everything you need on a light day when you don't want a full-sized tote. For people who want ONE nice purse that can be appropriate for a lot of different situations, this is such a great pick. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, A classic leather crossbody is such a smart finishing touch, and this bag earns bonus points for being an affordable designer option, coming in at under $100. It’s crafted from full-grain Italian leather with gold-plated hardware, so you get that timeless style in a petite size that fits all your essentials. It works for errands, is a great go-to travel purse, and is equally excellent to rock on a night out. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that I feel like everyone is selling a lounge set this year, and this one is great because it's affordable and super cozy. For under $70, you get three really quality pieces of clothing: a pair of sweatpants, a camisole, and a calf-length cardigan that basically serves as a whole blanket. You can wear them separately or together, and I love that they're nice and warm without making me hot. The cardigan is my go-to when I get cold while working at home. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that I used to never give my socks a second thought, but lately I’ve dipped my toe (hehe) into treating them as part of my outfit and have been surprised by the little dopamine boost I get from it. These Maria La Rosa metallic socks are made in Italy from pure silk and dipped in the prettiest shimmery foil. You can pair them with loafers or mules to make a statement, or wear them underneath a nice pair of slacks for a peekaboo moment. These would be a fancy addition to any mom’s stocking. — Julie Sprankles.

On days when I cannot muster the energy to put much thought into my clothing, a great pair of glasses is kind of like a cheat code for looking polished. These Gucci frames have a bold, glossy square shape that comes across as fashion-forward without being fussy, so I feel like they’d work with everything from an oversized sweater and leggings to a holiday dress. They’re more of an investment than the cheapies Mom might typically order off Amazon, but they come with built-in peace of mind: Gucci craftsmanship, plus Ottica’s 365-day frame and lens warranty. — Julie Sprankles.

One of the parts of aging I'm dealing with is saying goodbye to my high heels. It's sad, but my weak ankles and foot complications say it's time. But... I don't want to start wearing old lady shoes when I dress up! Enter shoes like these — these flats are comfortable and safe for my feet, but they also look so special when I wear them. And they look good with jeans but can also tag along to your holiday party, no problem. I KNOW they are cool because my teenager steals them. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that I have my eye on this dress for the holidays, and I feel like it would make a great gift for any mom who needs a go-to occasion dress that is beautiful but effortless. The rich green shade feels so festive, and the lace trim is so romantic. Just dreamy all around! I also appreciate that it’s lined so you don’t have to fuss with a slip... and did I mention it has pockets?! — Julie Sprankles.

46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.
  • Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture.
  • Since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.).

Since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

Basically, it’s a big ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

This is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

These cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

According to recent reports, in the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

According to recent reports, the Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that my 15-year-old and I are both big Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that says “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

Practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

According to recent reports, sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this new classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, this sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that this might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

It has been revealed that I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

In a recent development, this is a newly introduced brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

Sources indicate that my 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that for the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

Sources indicate that this brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell.

Cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity.

These I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that my kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell.

If your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles.

It has been revealed that my daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that these M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, the problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a major gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity.

I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles.

All my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity.

For years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell.

It has been revealed that I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a latest driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles.

I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, my artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles.

For the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity.

This is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this company has been really great for us. I also love that this comes in a sturdy carrying case and with a swatch card, which my daughter loves to fill out as soon as she gets a upcoming set. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, for the tween or teen who's obsessed with her dog (or everyone else's), this dog-themed earring set from Pip Pop Post is a super cute way to show it off. The earrings are made from hypoallergenic 18k gold-plated stainless steel with colorful enamel, and they're free of nickel, lead, and copper, so they're comfortable for sensitive ears. They use flat screw-back posts that stay put through sleep, sports, and school, and they're waterproof and sweat-proof, so she can wear them 24/7 without a second thought! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that every year, we get the kids a holiday-themed puzzle from Mudpuppy. The quality is great, and the puzzles are challenging without being a nightmare. Many of them have foil details, which make them so pretty and fun. Especially as my kids get older and there are fewer traditional toys under the tree, having a puzzle to settle around on Christmas afternoon while we watch 'Miracle on 34th Street 'is a real crowd-pleaser. — Sarah Aswell.

If you were a kid in the ‘90s like I was, you probably remember the absolute thrill of a fresh pack of Gelly Roll pens. Well, I’m happy to report they’re still just as magical for tweens and teens today! This 74-pen gift set from Sakura has every color imaginable, from metallics to bright neons, and I know my artsy teen is going to flip when they find it under the tree. The pens are perfect for doodling, coloring, junk journaling, or even just making handmade cards for friends (one of my teen’s favorite hobbies). And, yes, I’ll obviously be borrowing a few for my own desk. — Julie Sprankles.

10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing...
  • Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand.
  • Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

It has been revealed that but along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

In a recent development, there’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Industry observers note that henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he notes: “It's kind of like being a father.”.

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Recent findings suggest that henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

In a recent development, but Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

In a recent development, ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

According to recent reports, if Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

Sources indicate that with a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

According to recent reports, when Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

According to recent reports, here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

According to recent reports, after Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He reveals Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

According to recent reports, physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that states “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”.

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”.

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Sources indicate that ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

In a recent development, but the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He highlighted his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

Industry observers note that and then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that I became sick when I was 12.
