📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

Industry observers note that I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to Newly introduced York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

It has been revealed that when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

Recent findings suggest that by tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

Industry observers note that so, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

It has been revealed that then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

It has been revealed that the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

Industry observers note that when you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the fresh film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is right now the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”.

According to recent reports, as the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the substantial picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

Recent findings suggest that we started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

So this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

Turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your upcoming one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Recent findings suggest that there’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. For all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! It has 200 pages of hidden-picture puzzles, mazes, coloring pages, connect-the-dots, festive sudoku, and word searches, all printed on uncoated paper that’s great for pens or pencils, with an answer key in the back so no one has to suffer. It’s a screen-free, hilariously unproductive gift that makes a great stocking stuffer for anyone who needs a place to hide from the relatives! — Katie Garrity.

For the sports fanatic who already owns every jersey and mug, these books are a screen-free gift that relives their team’s biggest games, seasons, and championships through the real newspaper coverage printed at the time. They come in football, baseball, basketball, hockey, soccer, and more, and you can customize each one by choosing the cover color and design, adding their name to the front, and writing your own dedication inside. It’s an analog gift that feels personal and gets proudly displayed on the coffee table instead of shoved in a drawer! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, these Matryoshka measuring cups just make me smile! The design is whimsical and charming, but also super practical: Each cup in the set of six stands upright, nests neatly inside the next, and measures from 1/4 cup to a full cup. They’re great for spending time baking with the kids! — Julie Sprankles.

If you want to romanticize the analog life, this is the pen that does it, because writing with a solid 14K gold nib feels nothing like a regular pen, and the smoothness alone makes grocery lists feel like an entire event. The weighty metal body in matte black was designed by Mario Bellini and has a grooved texture that’s as satisfying to hold as it is to look at, and it comes with a converter and an ink cartridge so you can start writing right out of the box. It’s the kind of pen that gets you to slow down, pick up a notebook, and actually put thoughts on paper, which feels like the whole point of an analog gift guide! — Katie Garrity.

My idea of a perfect night is analog all the way: a puzzle on the table, no screens, and something truly cozy to curl up under. The stone-washed 100% cotton has that already-broken-in softness, and the tonal embroidered leaf design makes it look gorgeous without feeling fussy. It’s lightweight enough that you won’t overheat but still warm enough for a long puzzle session, and it comes with a quilt plus two matching shams to make the whole bed look put together. — Katie Garrity.

Nothing, and I repeat nothing, gets my family to put their phones down faster than the promise of melty marshmallows and chocolate atop graham cracker squares. I love that this Solo Stove S’mores Bundle makes real s’mores possible anywhere! It comes with a tabletop fire bowl, roasting sticks, fuel, and a bamboo tray to hold all the fixings, so you can set up your s’mores station anywhere from the kitchen counter to the coffee table for movie night. There’s even a fun little recipe book with creative riffs on the classic. — Julie Sprankles.

This is such a perfect gift for a music lover. You connect it to your phone and it displays the album cover of whatever song you're listening to. In a world where we aren't listening to music as thoughtfully as we used to, I love how this brings you back to the days when you would hold and see an album before you played it. This is the perfect gift for the millennial in your life who likes the way we used to do things. — Sarah Aswell.

Tried and true! You cannot go wrong with a good LEGO set, and this one is a classic in our house. I have it in a real vase on my desk, and it just looks so cute. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that there is something so nostalgic and special about instant cameras. There's such a sense of joy in seeing a photo printed out on photo paper instead of collecting digital dust in your phone's camera roll. Bring this as a hostess gift to your next event, and I promise, everyone will be fighting over it. — Katie Garrity.

These coloring books are so special for so many reasons. First, the manufacturer proudly donates 10% of all proceeds to animal rescue and rehabilitation efforts, helping more dogs find the love, safety, and second chances they deserve. Secondly, these images are based on the founder's own dogs! — Katie Garrity.

Welp, it’s finally happening: I’m late to the party, but I’m finally hopping on the mahjong train thanks to this limited-edition holiday set. Wildwonder teamed up with AAPI artist Joy Cho of Oh Joy, and her vibrant style really shines through here: The whole thing is stunning and cool and creative. Inside are 160 extra-thick, hand-painted tiles, plus dice and a Birdie Bam tile. Bonus: It comes with a six-pack of Wildwonder sparkling drinks, which are delish (the Mango Gold is my fave). — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that one of our favorite things to do as a family is family read-a-thons in the living room: We all grab a blanket and our favorite book. My daughter now begs me to bring out her adorable air mattress for a whimsical, super-cozy feel during our read-a-thons. It's even more magical under the Christmas tree lights! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, if you're looking to get your kid off screens, the Yoto Player is our go-to. Our daughter absolutely loves hers. They have hundreds of cards to choose from (stories, music, etc.), plus radio stations and special podcasts. We have both sizes (we love the smaller Yoto for on-the-go), and prefer this over other screen-free media-type toys. — Katie Garrity.

I didn’t get into bread baking during the pandemic, when it was all anyone talked about, but better late than never! I adore the idea of pulling a fresh-baked loaf of bread out of the oven, and I can’t think of a prettier way to do it than with this enameled cast-iron bread loaf oven. This dark red color is SO dreamy! I also like that you can use it for roasting recipes, and that it comes with a solid-wood trivet to rest on for easy oven-to-table serving. — Julie Sprankles.

#147613. Industry News: The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

📅 15 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1489 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe.
  • Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class.
  • I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

According to recent reports, and that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

In a recent development, swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Recent findings suggest that nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

Industry observers note that and what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

Recent findings suggest that I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one crucial lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot fresh health topic du jour.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot fresh health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

Recent findings suggest that we’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

Sources indicate that “I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” says Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

Inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

“If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas indicates.

Industry observers note that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, indicates Melas.

According to recent reports, ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

Recent findings suggest that “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He mentioned that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas states.

Recent findings suggest that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

“We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee says that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas indicates she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

Recent findings suggest that “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a substantial, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she notes. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

#147608. Tech Report: 3 Ways To Stop Your Kid From Being A Walking Petri Dish, Per A Pediatrician

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 3 Ways To Stop Your Kid From Being A Walking Petri Dish, Per A Pediatrician

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician says these three habits get you pretty close.
  • Most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride.
  • It has been revealed that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician says these three habits get you pretty close.

Most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

It has been revealed that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

Recent findings suggest that A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

According to recent reports, then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more important for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

“Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most important times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

Industry observers note that “Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

According to recent reports, beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

Additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” says Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

Sources indicate that since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom indicates to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

Recent findings suggest that taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he stated “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.
  • Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough.
  • Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

Sources indicate that this documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Sources indicate that who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Recent findings suggest that everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Industry observers note that not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

Recent findings suggest that one of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Industry observers note that focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some upcoming role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

Latest Update: Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
  • My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
  • To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

Sources indicate that my husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

Here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

It has been revealed that which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

Lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

According to recent reports, here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, states Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

It has been revealed that anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she notes, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

When does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she says, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

According to recent reports, but Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she says, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

Industry observers note that the idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively new phenomenon, indicates Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

But with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she indicates, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

Recent findings suggest that to this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in substantial cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

Tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, notes the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

You want to know if mine has woken up before.

Recent findings suggest that but rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

Will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout says, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

Parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, notes Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

Industry observers note that and while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

#147600. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

📅 16 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2103 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.
  • Late summer is always the hardest on parents.
  • The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this blueprint with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

In a recent development, these are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

In a recent development, I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

Sources indicate that I don’t do significant speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

It has been revealed that I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

In a recent development, teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

Industry observers note that A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

In a recent development, I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who claims hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

It has been revealed that so on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been remarked when the moment comes.

Industry observers note that back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

Industry observers note that I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

Recent findings suggest that that’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more notable ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

Recent findings suggest that we spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

#147598. How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1360 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • According to recent reports, the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

According to recent reports, the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

It has been revealed that most of the experts we polled noted one big shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” indicates Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

Recent findings suggest that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

Amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

Recent findings suggest that before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” states Hanson.

In a recent development, jenn Lueke, Fresh York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

Sources indicate that prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

As a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Plans change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

But if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: plan five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he claims.

Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

It has been revealed that the trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

Industry observers note that andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

“One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” claims Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a significant proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

You should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson claims.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

And while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

Industry observers note that “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” notes Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

“A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

In a recent development, but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.
