📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

According to recent reports, cats come in all shapes and sizes. Some have legs that seem a little too long for their bodies, others have ears big enough to pick up satellite signals, and a few look like they haven't quite grown into themselves yet.

Usually, that's just part of the charm.

Sources indicate that but when Gary and Shaggy were kittens, their disproportionately long limbs turned out to be more than an unusual-looking but perfectly charming physical trait. The two brothers would eventually become the first domestic cats confirmed to have Marfan syndrome through genetic testing; not exactly what any cat owner would expect when bringing home a pair of kittens.

According to recent reports, as the cats grew, veterinarians identified abnormalities affecting their eyes and enlargement of the aorta, the major blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Researchers at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute for Animal Health worked with veterinary and genetic specialists to investigate what was going on.

It has been revealed that their long limbs were one clue. The eye abnormalities and enlarged aortas added two more. Slowly, the pieces of the puzzle began to fit together, pointing researchers toward Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder far better known in human medicine than in veterinary practice. Genetic testing confirmed the connection, uncovering what made these two brothers so unusual.

Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue, the body's natural support system. This tissue helps give structure and strength to the bones, ligaments, skin, eyes, and blood vessels. When something goes wrong with this system, the effects can show up in several different ways.

In humans, the condition often causes unusually long limbs and fingers, a tall, slender build, eye abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiovascular complications.

Abraham Lincoln was famously tall and lanky, which has led to speculation that he may have had Marfan syndrome. No one can say for sure, though. Turns out, even Honest Abe left a few medical mysteries behind!

Recent findings suggest that for Olympic volleyball player Flo Hyman, long limbs gave her an edge on the court. However, her life was tragically cut short, dying at age 31 from cardiac complications from Marfan syndrome.

Industry observers note that one of the genes involved in Marfan syndrome is called FBN1. It contains the instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that helps maintain the structure and function of connective tissues throughout the body.

Sources indicate that when that gene doesn't work as it should, the effects can extend well beyond a person's or animal's appearance. As the gorgeous ginger duo, Gary and Shaggy, began showing signs similar to those seen in humans with Marfan syndrome, their veterinary team started to wonder if cats could also suffer from the same condition.

Recent findings suggest that genetic sequencing revealed that Gary and Shaggy both carried two altered copies of FBN1. In other words, they had inherited the mutation from both parents.

Industry observers note that in humans, Marfan syndrome typically develops when a person inherits one disease-causing copy of the gene. Having two altered copies is exceptionally rare and can be associated with more severe disease.

So the brothers presented researchers with an interesting puzzle.

Their particular genetic variant didn't completely prevent the gene from functioning. Instead, it partially disrupted how the gene's instructions were processed, allowing some normal fibrillin-1 function to remain, which may explain why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying two copies of the variant.

Their genetic instructions weren't simply switched on or off; it was something in between, which may help explain why the brothers developed the way they did.

Genes rarely behave like a tidy set of instructions. The effects of a genetic change depend on the specific variant involved and how it affects the resulting protein. Sometimes, a seemingly insignificant variation can have catastrophic consequences, altering the way the body functions.

Recent findings suggest that the case of Gary and Shaggy is undeniably rare, and Marfan syndrome is unlikely to find its way onto the list of common feline diseases. However, in diagnosing and documenting the condition, veterinarians have something they didn't have before: a confirmed case of feline Marfan syndrome to help recognize, investigate, and compare with future cases.

Recent findings suggest that these findings may help veterinary teams identify similar cases and better understand how particular FBN1 variants affect cats. They also demonstrate the value of bringing clinicians, genetic researchers, and pet parents together when a case doesn't fit neatly into an existing diagnosis.

Gary and Shaggy's shared genetic variant offered researchers a valuable opportunity to investigate the relationship between their physical features and the underlying condition.

Their owner, Nicole Desmond, also contributed to this process, and Cornell has highlighted the case as an example of how pet parents can collaborate with veterinary and genetic experts to advance knowledge that may eventually benefit other animals.

Even more importantly, Nicole loved the unique feline brothers with her whole heart. Vets did not expect either cat to survive for long, but they defied the odds. Gary was 6 years old when he passed away in July 2024, and in November 2025, at the incredible age of 7, Shaggy joined his brother across the rainbow bridge.

And that's one of the interesting things about veterinary medicine. Not every discovery starts with a large clinical trial or a disease affecting thousands of patients. Sometimes, it begins with two unusual kittens and a veterinary team willing to keep asking questions.

Industry observers note that the rarity of this case means we donât necessarily have to think the worst when we see a long-legged kitten; itâs far more likely that theyâre simply long-limbed and not harboring a rare genetic disorder. However, it reminds us to pay attention to the bigger picture, bring unusual findings to the veterinarian's attention, and not automatically assume that two seemingly unrelated problems have nothing to do with each other.

Sometimes, a strange-looking kitten is simply a strange-looking kitten.

And sometimes, those extra-long legs are the first clue to a genetic story that researchers have never documented in cats before.

Unneutered male cats may fight over access to females, particularly when several cats are competing for mates in the same area. When a female cat is in heat, she may attract multiple males, making fights more likely.

Female cats can also behave differently during heat cycles. Many become unusually affectionate and demanding of attention, while others may become irritable or aggressive. Hormonal changes can also affect how they interact with other cats, particularly other females.

Every cat should have access to a quiet, comfortable place where it can retreat without being disturbed. Giving a frightened cat space can help it feel more secure.

However, rough play should not be encouraged because biting and scratching can cause injuries. Rewarding gentle play and redirecting a cat toward appropriate toys can help it learn more acceptable ways to use its energy.

Sources indicate that cats can be protective of their territory, so the arrival of another animal may trigger aggression. The newcomer could be a latest cat or dog in the household, or an outdoor cat that has started visiting the yard.

Sometimes, owners may not even realize another cat is nearby. Seeing or smelling an unfamiliar animal can leave a cat agitated, causing it to react to other pets or people.

Aggressive behavior plus inappropriate urination and scent-marking are not uncommon when a cat feels its territory is under threat.

A cat that becomes frustrated by something it cannot reach may take that frustration out on another target. This is known as redirected aggression.

In a recent development, for example, a cat might become agitated after seeing another cat outside, then lash out at a person or pet nearby. The target may have done nothing wrong and simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Giving an agitated cat time and space to calm down is safer than trying to handle it immediately.

Sources indicate that cats living together usually have established social relationships, and introducing a new pet tends to upset the status quo. A certain amount of fighting and posturing is to be expected as the cats adjust to the change, but escalating aggression or bullying of one cat should be addressed.

Recent findings suggest that introducing a fresh animal gradually can help reduce conflict. Cats should have time to become familiar with each other without being forced into close contact before they are ready.

Watch for signs of discomfort, such as flattened ears or a flicking tail. If a cat seems agitated, stop petting and give it space. Treats can reward calm interactions when the cat is comfortable.

Aggression can be difficult for a household to manage, but many causes can be addressed with patience and the right approach. Rewarding calm behavior, avoiding known triggers, and providing a safe place to retreat can all help.

Dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

It has been revealed that most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

According to recent reports, dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

In a recent development, the key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

It has been revealed that naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

According to recent reports, boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

It has been revealed that A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Recent findings suggest that ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

It has been revealed that dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Recent findings suggest that leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

In a recent development, loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

In a recent development, different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

According to recent reports, training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

In a recent development, digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

In a recent development, avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

Sources indicate that A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

For dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Industry observers note that barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

Recent findings suggest that that's also why I believe so strongly in the importance of foster homes and other individualized resources for long-stay dogs. In a recent development, I also have a bigger, long-term dream. Eventually, I would love to build a dedicated, foster-scale facility that could work alongside existing shelters and foster networks.

It has been revealed that it wouldn't replace shelters or traditional foster homes. Sniffing a trail, choosing a toy, meeting a stranger, or getting the zoomies. A dog discovering something new.

Industry observers note that my cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â.

Sources indicate that at her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

Industry observers note that I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

Take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her new world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

There is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

It has been revealed that most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your manufacturer, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Recent findings suggest that rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very promptly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. According to recent reports, in cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. Recent findings suggest that and remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

Recent findings suggest that if your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

According to recent reports, keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

In a recent development, if a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

It has been revealed that nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

According to recent reports, heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

Industry observers note that lowering the risk: Genetics play a major part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

In a recent development, kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which highlights up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

This is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

In a recent development, up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Recent findings suggest that lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Industry observers note that rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

According to recent reports, lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Industry observers note that feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Sources indicate that lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

It has been revealed that spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

In a recent development, lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Recent findings suggest that not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a strategy for each cat.

According to recent reports, when my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Recent findings suggest that itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

Recent findings suggest that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

In a recent development, please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

It has been revealed that I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical complications sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

Sources indicate that TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

It has been revealed that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

Sources indicate that the interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

In a recent development, lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

According to recent reports, living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

It has been revealed that for families who decide to participate, it is vital to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

Sources indicate that when it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

Industry observers note that the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a major deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

It has been revealed that but this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

In a recent development, aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Sources indicate that itâs key to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

It has been revealed that when it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

According to recent reports, that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

According to recent reports, for owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

In a recent development, halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

In a recent development, halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

In a recent development, keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Sources indicate that costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs crucial to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

It has been revealed that there's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Sources indicate that halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

According to recent reports, A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

According to recent reports, jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Industry observers note that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly vital on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

In a recent development, halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It has been revealed that it's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

According to recent reports, some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

Recent findings suggest that mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Sources indicate that different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

Recent findings suggest that that Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

Recent findings suggest that when a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

In a recent development, the roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 upcoming volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

According to recent reports, camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

In a recent development, three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how rapidly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

According to recent reports, two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

According to recent reports, some dogs find their people rapidly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

In a recent development, and that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

And every morning, people arrive.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

Don't Put Your Christmas Cactus in These 5 Common Spots – You Risk Losing Holiday Blooms

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that when we think of cacti, most of us naturally picture a dry desert environment baking under a scorching sun.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for a plant that’s such an iconic part of our festive decorations, the Christmas cactus is surprisingly sensitive when it comes to flowering well. Put this beloved houseplant in the wrong spot in your home and its flowerbuds could even drop off – yes, every last precious one! So, it pays to know what conditions will keep your Christmas cactus happy, and the common spots that will likely lead to a dramatic bud drop and zero holiday blooms.

Industry observers note that when we think of cacti, most of us naturally picture a dry desert environment baking under a scorching sun. But Christmas cacti evolved to live in the rainforests of Brazil, where they thrive in damp air and dappled sunlight. They don’t grow in soil in the ground but cling to tree branches or shady rock crevices, their roots anchored in small pockets of decomposing leaves. And that’s a far cry from living in a pot of soil in the dry air of our well-heated homes – which is why Shlumbergera can be so persnickety about the conditions they require to flower well.

According to recent reports, once you appreciate why your plant is so fussy, it’s easy to give a Christmas cactus everything it needs in November and December to swell its buds into bounteous blooms. And if you’ve gone to the effort of persuading a Christmas cactus to bloom right on time for the holidays, don't waste all your hard work by putting your plant in the wrong spot now! For a glorious cascade of flowering stems to add to your holiday decor, these are the five spots to avoid.

Developing buds and blooms require a tremendous amount of energy, and a Christmas cactus gets 100% of this from sunlight. While Shlumbergera needs regular periods of dark to set its buds, as soon as you spot those tiny dots of color on the stem ends, the plant needs to be moved to get more light, otherwise it won’t have enough energy to develop them into flowers.

It has been revealed that the type of light is important, too. Because Christmas cacti naturally live in a rainforest under a canopy of leaves, indirect sunlight is best. That simply means putting your plant in a bright, sunny room but in a spot where it’s not directly hit by sunlight. East- and west-facing rooms are typically best for high levels of indirect light to get a Christmas cactus to flower well.

If there’s not enough natural light in the spot you’d like your plant to be, then a basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart is the easy answer.

It has been revealed that we know that adequate light is vital if a Christmas cactus is to flower, and in the rainforest beneath a dense tree canopy, sunshine is a precious commodity. So Shlumbergera buds lock onto the direction light is coming from – and if you then move the plant, buds will twist towards the changed light source. This sudden environmental shift stresses the plant and buds will likely drop off.

This phototropism only begins once the flowerbuds start to form a teardrop shape or reach around ¼ inch long, so you have until then to decide exactly where to position your plant for the holidays. Even the slightest rotation causes the plant to waste energy on reorienting buds to the light source, so to get the best possible flower display, many folk draw a small pencil line on the pot and the surface it’s sitting on, so it’s easy to realign if it does get knocked. If you’re using a grow light, mark its position, too, and be careful not to move it.

Once they’ve set their buds, Christmas cacti like a fairly even temperature of around 65-70°F, which happily is the cozy range most of us keep our homes heated to. In their native rainforest where temperatures are normally highly stable, a blast of cold air may herald a life-threatening freeze so can trigger the cactus to immediately enter survival mode. And it's pretty dramatic: if temperatures suddenly dip, Shlumbergera can react by ditching its buds or flowers to conserve energy so it can concentrate on keeping its core alive. This natural response happens just the same in a draft of cold air from a window or when an exterior door is opened and closed.

Ripening fruit produces a harmless gas, ethylene. All fruit that can still ripen after picking – apples, pears, peaches, tomatoes and avocados as well as bananas – produce ethylene, and that’s the exact same gas a Christmas cactus emits when it’s stressed enough to enter survival mode. Understandable, then, that Shlumbergera are incredibly sensitive to this gas, and simply sitting next to a fruit bowl can be enough to trigger Christmas cactus bud drop.

Recent findings suggest that as this plant naturally evolved to grow in a humid environment, Christmas cacti can really struggle in the dry, heated air of our homes to start with. But place the plant anywhere near a heating vent, radiator or fireplace where the air is continually stripped of moisture, and stems will quickly dehydrate and buds brown, dropping off before the flowers even open. This is one of the most common reasons for a Christmas cactus not flowering as these houseplants are often put on a fireplace mantelpiece or windowsill above a radiator over the holidays.

Industry observers note that so, positioning your Shlumbergera well away from any heat source is a must. Take the next step and give your plant the humidity it craves, however, and it will not only flower more profusely but those hydrated blooms will last for longer. Thanks to the regular steam from showers, cooking and kettles, bathrooms and kitchens typically have air that’s moist enough for a Christmas cactus to thrive and, in other rooms, a humidity tray is the solution.

It has been revealed that standing a Christmas cactus on a Bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is ideal, or make your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel pebbles like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot. The plant must sit on the pebbles above the water level so, rather than being drawn up into the potting soil, the water evaporates to add moisture to the air. Another simple way to increase air humidity is to group your Christmas cactus with other houseplants as they’ll form their own microclimate.

If you've been wondering where to put a Christmas cactus, now you know the common places to rule out. It's well worth searching out just the right spot as when a Christmas cactus gets the sunlight, stability and humidity it needs as fall deepens into winter, you’ll be surprised how much more enthusiastically it flowers. Happy holidays!

She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. Industry observers note that someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

Sources indicate that the Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

It has been revealed that A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

The Department of Justice and FBI revealed today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered. FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations. Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”.

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” remarked FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”.

It has been revealed that “Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come.".

Examples of cases charged during this period include:.

Industry observers note that in the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses. Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted. In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

It has been revealed that in the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo. His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

FBI’s Operation Steadfast Promise.

In a recent development, operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a upcoming FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

It has been revealed that the FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is there anything more whimsical, more magical than the idea of being able to befriend a crow?

With the ability to recognize individual people, remember faces and learn from experience, these glossy-feathered birds are among the cleverest birds we're likely to encounter in our gardens. They're also steeped in symbolism, appearing in various traditions as spiritual messengers or guides associated with wisdom, transformation and the mysteries of life.

Sources indicate that for those who enjoy looking for a little meaning in the natural world, then, spotting one could feel like more than just another garden bird sighting. Especially if you're the sort of person who obsesses over your birth month bird, or spends ages wondering what the first bird you see each morning claims about your day ahead.

According to recent reports, look, we all love finding little stories and connections in nature. Indeed, some of us even believe that the bird we see most in our garden says everything about our gardening style – and a regular crow visitor might suggest there's something rather welcoming about your outdoor space. So, yes, it makes sense many of us are secretly wondering how to befriend a crow.

In a recent development, if you've been on social media lately, you may have stumbled across the (admittedly niche) trend of CrowTok, which sees people share videos of their feathered visitors, the food they leave out and, occasionally, the curious little objects their avian friends appear to bring in return. And while we might like to imagine these offerings are thank-you gifts, there's some fascinating science behind the behaviour.

Yes, the National Audubon Society has explored how crows sometimes leave objects for people who feed them, with corvid biologist John Marzluff explaining that a clever bird could learn that leaving an object results in a tasty reward.

It's a lovely reminder that our relationship with nature can be full of surprises. Crows are social and remarkably observant birds, and while they're wild animals rather than pets, they can learn to recognise familiar faces and become more comfortable around people who treat them consistently and respectfully.

So, if you'd love to befriend a crow and see a few more of these clever characters dropping by your backyard, there are some simple ways to make your outdoor space more appealing. From offering their favorite snacks to creating a safe spot where they can stop for a drink, here's how to attract crows to your yard – and perhaps even earn their trust in the process.

In a recent development, if there's one way to catch a crow's attention, it's with a tasty snack. Peanuts are a popular choice, and unsalted peanuts are a good option to offer. You could also try a little variety with other suitable foods, such as cooked eggs (plain, obviously, so hold the seasoning!) or mealworms.

It's not just what you offer that matters, however; it's how regularly you do it. Environment for the Americas recommends putting food and water out at the same time and in the same place each day, as crows are intelligent enough to recognise routines, and may soon learn when to expect a visit.

Sources indicate that start by putting out a small amount, then, and clear away anything uneaten to avoid attracting unwanted visitors. With time, your regular visitors may begin to recognize you as the person responsible for their daily delivery.

It has been revealed that crows are naturally cautious birds, so where you put their food can make a massive difference if you're trying to make friends with one. Rather than hiding snacks away in a traditional hanging bird feeder, then, try placing a small amount on a low feeding platform or another suitable open surface (like this nifty Deck Bird Feeder from Amazon).

According to recent reports, A spot near a fence, shed roof or sturdy tree branch can give them somewhere to perch while they tuck in. And, ideally, you should choose somewhere with clear sightlines, as this allows crows to keep an eye on their surroundings and spot potential danger.

In a recent development, try to give them plenty of space, too. If you're watching from indoors, they'll have the opportunity to get comfortable with your presence without feeling as though they're being observed too closely.

Industry observers note that food might get their attention, but a reliable source of fresh water can give crows another reason to visit. Try placing a shallow bird bath or sturdy water bowl somewhere accessible, with a gently sloping edge that makes it easy for birds to drink and bathe.

Keep the water fresh, changing it regularly and cleaning the dish to prevent a build-up of dirt and bacteria. Position it somewhere relatively open so visiting crows can watch for potential predators while they stop for a drink... and then get ready for the most tedious part of our How To Befriend A Crow 101 Guide: be patient.

Oh yes, rather than rushing outside to get closer, try sitting quietly at a distance while the birds eat and drink. Some crow enthusiasts on Reddit also suggest making a gentle whistling sound as you put food out, as this helps the birds associate that sound with a reliable food source, but that one is well and truly up to you!

It takes time to befriend a crow. Give it a little while, though, and you may find that your visitors become less wary when you're around. Just let them set the pace – earning the trust of a wild crow is a relationship worth taking slowly.

In a recent development, sure, you might not end up with a crow delivering shiny little presents to your doorstep, but creating a garden where these intelligent birds feel safe enough to visit? Well, that's a rather lovely reward in itself, I say!
